reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / Yen and Jaffe's Reproductive Endocrinology
clinicalPearls: The condition features nests of luteinised theca cells scattered through the ovarian stroma, driving marked ovarian androgen production
Hyperandrogenism is typically more severe than in polycystic ovary syndrome and often produces frank virilisation, with hirsutism, temporal balding, deepening of the voice, and clitoromegaly
It is strongly linked to insulin resistance and hyperinsulinaemia, and may present as part of the HAIR-AN phenotype with acanthosis nigricans
It is most often recognised in peri- and postmenopausal women but also occurs in younger women, in whom it can be mistaken for severe polycystic ovary syndrome
Serum testosterone is usually substantially elevated, and a key task is to distinguish it from an androgen-secreting ovarian or adrenal tumour
Diagnosis integrates the clinical picture with hormonal profiling and imaging, since ovaries may be enlarged and solid rather than polycystic in appearance

Management options include suppression of ovarian androgen output with a GnRH agonist, insulin-sensitising strategies, and bilateral oophorectomy in postmenopausal women when malignancy must be excluded or symptoms are severe
reference.pathophysiology: Ovarian hyperthecosis is a non-neoplastic disorder in which islands of luteinised theca-type cells are distributed throughout the ovarian stroma and secrete androgens, chiefly testosterone. Unlike the follicle-based dysfunction of polycystic ovary syndrome, the androgen excess here arises from these stromal luteinised cells, whose activity is amplified by hyperinsulinaemia; insulin and insulin-like growth factor stimulate ovarian theca and stromal cells to produce androgens, creating a self-reinforcing link between insulin resistance and hyperandrogenism. The resulting high circulating testosterone produces the virilising features. Because the androgen source is diffuse ovarian stroma rather than a discrete mass, imaging typically shows bilaterally enlarged solid ovaries rather than a tumour.
additionalDifferentials: Androgen-secreting ovarian tumour (e.g. Sertoli-Leydig cell tumour)
additionalInvestigations: Serum total testosterone and other androgens to quantify hyperandrogenism
Assessment for insulin resistance, including fasting glucose and lipid profile
Transvaginal or pelvic ultrasound to assess ovarian size and morphology
Cross-sectional imaging of the adrenals and ovaries if a tumour is suspected
17-hydroxyprogesterone and adrenal workup to exclude congenital adrenal hyperplasia and Cushing syndrome
Gonadotrophin measurement to help interpret the hormonal picture
redFlags: Rapid onset or rapidly progressive virilisation suggesting an androgen-secreting tumour
Very high serum testosterone raising concern for a neoplastic source
A discrete ovarian or adrenal mass on imaging
Symptoms or signs suggesting coexisting Cushing syndrome
reference.prognosis: The condition itself is benign, but it causes considerable distress from virilisation and carries the metabolic consequences of associated insulin resistance, including increased cardiometabolic risk. Androgen suppression or oophorectomy can control hyperandrogenism, and addressing insulin resistance improves the broader metabolic profile.
pitfalls: Labelling the presentation as polycystic ovary syndrome despite disproportionately severe virilisation and testosterone elevation
Failing to exclude an androgen-secreting tumour before attributing symptoms to hyperthecosis
Neglecting the associated insulin resistance and its cardiometabolic implications
Expecting a polycystic appearance on imaging when the ovaries are typically enlarged and solid
management: Suppress ovarian androgen production with a GnRH agonist or, in the appropriate patient, a combined oral contraceptive to lower circulating testosterone
Add an anti-androgen such as spironolactone or cyproterone acetate to control hirsutism and virilisation, with mechanical and cosmetic hair-reduction measures

Offer bilateral oophorectomy as definitive treatment where fertility is not desired, particularly in peri- and postmenopausal women, since the diffuse stromal source responds poorly to medical therapy alone
Address the underlying insulin resistance with lifestyle modification and an insulin sensitiser such as metformin, given the self-reinforcing hyperinsulinaemia and hyperandrogenism link
Manage associated cardiometabolic risk by treating dyslipidaemia, dysglycaemia and hypertension and monitoring weight and glycaemic status
Maintain surveillance to distinguish and exclude an androgen-secreting ovarian or adrenal tumour with cross-sectional imaging and biochemical follow-up
Refer to reproductive endocrinology, with gynaecology input for surgical decisions and psychological support for distressing virilisation
